The margin arithmetic is already visible before any tariff help, with Wood Products EBITDA at $52.4M in Q2 against $37.3M a year earlier on plywood pricing up 15% y/y; the segment s weak spot was EWP, where I-joist pricing fell 7% and LVL 4% against Canadian import competition that now carries a 50% duty. key_risk: Housing demand, which is the whole bear case. Tariffs raise panel prices, but if starts roll over under a Fed that the market gives a one-in-three chance of hiking in September, BCC loses on volume what it gains on price — and its Building Materials Distribution arm, which produced the larger $85.6M of Q2 segment EBITDA, actually pays the higher input costs. counter_argument: The honest hazard in this specific recommendation is that it converts an existing 81.00 swing long with a 76.00 stop into a stop-free long-term hold, which is the classic way a trader launders a losing trade into an investment. The 76.00 stop is being removed deliberately and the invalidation below replaces it. If US housing starts fall more than 10% year-over-year for two consecutive months, or Wood Products segment EBITDA fails to exceed the $52.4M Q2 print in either Q3 or Q4 despite the tariff, the thesis is wrong and the position should be sold regardless of price.

catalyst.event: Jackson Hole keynote by Fed Chair Kevin Warsh, Friday morning 2026-08-28 — his first as chair — then the FOMC decision 2026-09-16. August CPI lands about 2026-09-10, in between.
catalyst.action: WAIT. Do not front-run the speech. Buy only into a hawkish Warsh, which should reprice this contract into the high 40s, and pass entirely on a neutral or dovish one.

thesis: The September FOMC market prices a 25bp hike at 33 bid / 34 ask against a cut at 0-1c, and the case that it is a little cheap is real: core PCE is 3.3% against an effective funds rate of 3.63%, so the real policy rate is roughly 0.3%; unemployment fell to 4.1% from 4.2%; the 2-year at 4.24% sits 61bp above the funds rate, which is the bond market already pricing tightening; and a fresh tariff-driven price impulse lands in the data window, with 50% US tariffs on $20B of Canadian goods effective 2026-08-23 and Canadian retaliation on 2026-09-08, both feeding an August CPI released roughly six days before the meeting. Warsh said at the July FOMC that the Fed will not hesitate to stop inflation.
key_risk: The evidence is thin and one-sided, which is exactly why this is conviction 2 and sized as a lottery ticket. The honest problem is that the rest of the curve is already coherent with 33c: Kalshi prices October at 22-23c and December at 24-28c, which compounds to roughly a two-in-three chance of at least one hike by year-end — consistent with a 2-year 61bp over funds. That means the market is not obviously mispricing September specifically, only distributing the hike across meetings, and I cannot demonstrate that September is the one.
counter_argument: Warsh has publicly argued that AI-driven productivity gains are disinflationary, which if developed at Jackson Hole is a direct dovish surprise against this position, and 69% of surveyed fund managers already expect a neutral tone. The Fed also rarely hikes without telegraphing, and the only telegraph opportunity before 2026-09-16 is Friday. That is precisely why the recommendation is to wait for Friday rather than to buy at 34 today — the speech is the thesis, not the setup.

counter_argument: The strongest case against is that merchant power margins are cyclical and the datacenter load story is the same story that carried this complex into a bubble which has since lost 70-85% in its speculative names; a 38% de-rating in Vistra may be the first leg of that repricing rather than the end of it. Invalidation, replacing a stop: if Vistra cuts or withdraws its 2026 adjusted EBITDA guidance of $6.8-7.6B, or if adjusted FCF before growth comes in below the $3.925B low end for two consecutive quarters, the thesis is wrong and the position should be sold regardless of price.
